Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 63
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Community Organizer
  trauma_type: Life-threatening accident
  pcl5: 49

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Expressions of Anger: Other people expressing anger, even calmly, Intrusive Thoughts: Unwanted thoughts, Visual (Uniforms): Military or police uniforms
  Memory: Partial Clarity: Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank, Memory Gaps: There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try, Cannot Find Words: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it
  Negative Appraisals: Emotional Numbness: I feel dead inside, Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted, Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe

Vignette:
Six months ago, Hemi’s truck slid off a rain-slicked county road, the guardrail tearing through the driver’s side window with a sound like ripping canvas. The moments inside the wreck were sharp and unblinking: the spray of shattered glass catching the gray sky, the way his own hands gripped the steering wheel until his knuckles blanched, the sudden, deafening silence when the engine died. Between the skid and the arrival of the first responders, however, there was a long, dark stretch he could not reach no matter how hard he tried. He knew he had done something wrong in that time, a mistake in how he had braced himself or corrected the slide, but the language to name it had slipped away. He could feel the weight of the accident in his chest, yet the words to describe the collapse of the frame or the smell of burning coolant remained just out of reach. Because the crash had been met by county emergency crews who arrived in dark blue uniforms with silver badges, and because the site foreman who later questioned him about the missed work orders had raised his voice until his face flushed, Hemi had come to associate authority and steady tones of displeasure with sudden, inescapable danger. When a volunteer at his organizing table calmly but firmly corrected a misplaced sign-in sheet, Hemi’s breath caught in his throat, his shoulders hiking up before he could look away. On the news, a distant report of a police pursuit left his stomach tightening around his ribs. The uniforms that flashed in his mind were not the men who had pulled him from the cab, but officers and soldiers he had never met, appearing unbidden in the margins of his vision whenever he tried to sort through community grant applications. As a community organizer coordinating tenant meetings and neighborhood safety workshops, Hemi’s work required him to stand in crowded rooms, listen to grievances, and navigate competing priorities. He began stepping out of the room when discussions grew heated, telling himself he needed to check on paperwork or make a phone call. He stopped attending the monthly coalition meetings where law enforcement liaisons sometimes spoke about local patrols, finding instead that he could only function when the agenda was strictly logistical. Over the weeks, his colleagues noticed he was disappearing from conversations that required quick decisions. He declined a promotion to lead the regional outreach initiative, citing fatigue, though what kept him sitting in his quiet office instead of walking the floor was the certainty that if he lost control of a situation, the same invisible fault would open up beneath his feet. Hemi had come to believe the wreck happened because of the way he had handled the wheel. This conviction sat alongside the way his body kept reacting as if he were still trapped in the crumpled cab; his pulse would race when a coffee cup clattered against a saucer, his muscles would lock when a door slammed, and his breath would shorten until he had to step outside for air. Yet beneath the constant tension, he felt dead inside, as though a heavy blanket had been laid over his capacity to care. He went to the grocery store, signed the permission slips for his nieces, and answered his phone, but the tasks felt performed by someone else. He told himself he was protecting himself from making another mistake, that staying quiet and moving slowly was the only way to keep the ground from giving way again. What finally brought him to the clinic was the way he could no longer sit through his own birthday dinner, flinching when a guest’s tone turned sharp across the table. He sat on the edge of the intake chair now, hands folded tightly in his lap, wondering if the numbness would ever lift or if he would spend the rest of his life bracing for the next sudden impact. He hoped someone could help him understand why his body still sounded the alarm, and what he might have done to finally let go of the guilt that had become his quiet companion.
